## The mechanism

`harness_shared.stamp_local_federated_write()` is a **BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE** trigger on
~18 federated CDC tables. On an UPDATE whose `fed_ts` is unchanged it treats the write as
local, and decides whether to re-stamp the LWW clock by diffing the row against a mask:

```sql
IF (to_jsonb(NEW) - <mask>) IS DISTINCT FROM (to_jsonb(OLD) - <mask>) THEN
  NEW.fed_ts := ...; NEW.fed_hlc := hlc_now(); NEW.origin := 'local';
END IF;
```

PostgreSQL computes a **STORED generated column after every BEFORE ROW trigger finishes**.
So inside this trigger:

- `to_jsonb(NEW)->>'<gencol>'` is **NULL** — it has not been computed yet;
- `to_jsonb(OLD)->>'<gencol>'` is the **already-stored value**.

Any generated column not in the mask therefore makes the diff fire on **every** update to
that table, including a byte-identical re-apply of the same remote op (a retry, a second
drain pass, a backfill re-scan). The trigger then relabels a remote peer's row
`origin='local'` and gives it a locally-generated clock that is **newer than the wire**.

## Why it is so much worse than it looks

The corruption is permanent and self-sealing. Every later redelivery of the publisher's
genuine op carries the older wire clock, loses the `fed_order_key(fed_hlc, fed_ts)`
compare, and is discarded. Nothing repairs it — not a retry, not a re-publish, not a
restart. The database looks settled; the only symptom is a probe asserting
`origin='remote'` mysteriously failing on a row that plainly arrived.

That invisibility is why WI-6210 survived four gate runs and three wrong diagnoses.

## It has happened three times

| # | column | table | fixed by |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `_search` | harness_plans, work_items, engineer_issues | mig 214/517 |
| 2 | `fed_key` | `plan_item_assignments` | mig 653 |
| 3 | `offer_fed_key` | `p2p_work_offers` | mig 681 |

Each of the first two was fixed by **adding one more column name to the mask**. Migration
653 even asserted, "verified by grep across every CDC table's DDL", that its column was the
last one — the grep matched the literal `fed_key`, and the next occurrence was named
`offer_fed_key`.

**Migration 681 stops naming them.** It derives the set from the catalog for the triggering
table (`pg_attribute.attgenerated <> ''`) and subtracts all of it, so a table that adds a
generated column under any name is covered on day one.

## If you touch this trigger

- **Never hand-list a generated column.** If you find yourself adding `- 'some_key'` to the
  mask, the generic subtraction is already there and something else is wrong.
- **The function is defined by a chain of full-body `CREATE OR REPLACE` migrations**
  (314/490 → 517 → 528 → 653 → 681). It has been damaged **twice** by replacing the whole
  body from a stale copy: 517 dropped 528's HLC work, and 653 dropped the `hlc_recv()`
  recv-advance 528 had restored (WI-6249). Before you replace it, diff against the *current
  highest-numbered* definition, not the one you remember.
- **Do not trust a test that inlines a copy of the trigger.** The pre-existing
  `plan-item-assignments.integration.test.ts` fixture pastes a hand-copy of the function
  body, so it keeps passing no matter what the shipped function later becomes — it tests the
  copy. `stamp-local-federated-write-generated-cols.integration.test.ts` loads the real body
  from the highest-numbered migration on disk instead, and uses a **novel** generated-column
  name so it proves catalog-masking rather than re-proving the last fix. It carries a teeth
  seam:

  ```bash
  STAMP_FN_MIGRATION=653-fed-key-generated-col-stamp-mask.sql \
    npm run test:file -- packages/operator-core/lib/sync/hyperbee/projections/__tests__/stamp-local-federated-write-generated-cols.integration.test.ts
  ```

  must go RED with `expected 'local' to be 'remote'`. A guard nobody has watched fail is not
  a guard.

## The debugging lesson

Three hypotheses were spent on the TypeScript apply path (un-threaded `applyOpVia`, a
capture echo, the forgeable `writerPubkey`) before anyone suspected the trigger. What ended
it was building instruments whose **silence was informative**:

- a detector keyed on the *condition* that defines the failure (`ownLogKeyHex === undefined`
  on a `skipOwnOps` put) rather than on the function suspected of causing it — it fired
  **zero** times in a bundle verified to contain it, which *refuted* the hypothesis instead
  of merely failing to confirm it;
- an echo probe on a different limb (frame a's own outbox), so the two together partitioned
  the remaining space: populated ⇒ capture, empty ⇒ apply.

Both came back negative, and *that* is what forced the search out of the TypeScript and into
the trigger. Before spending a run on a probe, ask what its silence would prove — and verify
the instrument is actually present in the artifact under test (grep the built bundle, check
its mtime) before reading a null result as evidence.
